extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, metaphysics, and natural history (readers of systematic philosophy of nature)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and metaphysical criteria for explaining organised nature and biological form from the standpoint of a metaphysical system that posits a will as the basis of nature; includes how to deploy final vs efficient causes, homology, and how to treat apparent exceptions. Useful for constructing or evaluating teleological and metaphysical explanations of organisms and their parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile determinism in action with freedom in being
rubrics_metrics.description: Every being without exception acts with strict necessity (the action follows from character and motives), while the being and nature (Esse) of things is the manifestation of a free will; therefore necessity belongs to Operari (doing) and freedom to Esse (being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This placement 'solves' the traditional riddle by attributing necessity to action and freedom to existence; when evaluating a philosophical account, check whether it preserves strict causal necessity of actions while locating freedom in the metaphysical status of being rather than in the contingent action. Anti-pattern: seeking freedom as an exception in the causal chain of actions rather than as a feature of thing-in-itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat multiplicity as phenomenal and the will as metaphysical unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplicity (the manifold of separate beings) is rooted in the forms of perception (space and time) and is foreign to the thing-in-itself; immediately known is only one being—one will—while plurality is an appearance produced by the intellect's forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations should account for apparent plurality as a product of subjectivity (space/time) and explain unity beneath phenomena. Use this principle when preferring unified metaphysical accounts over pluralistic ontologies that treat multiplicity as ultimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use teleology (final causes) as the primary guide for organised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The adaptation of parts to ends in organised beings makes teleology—a doctrine of final causes—a 'perfectly safe guide' for considering organised nature; final causes are the clue to understanding organised nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining anatomical or physiological form, prioritize accounts of ends and purposes. Scoring/evaluation: teleological explanations that coherently relate parts to organismal ends score higher for explanatory adequacy in this framework. Anti-pattern: attempting to explain organic form solely by mechanical efficient causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer aimlessness from failure to see a use
rubrics_metrics.description: If in some animal a part is found of which we do not see any use, we must never conjecture that nature produced it aimlessly or from caprice; assume it serves the will/foundation of the organism and continue seeking its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'unknown-use' organs (spleen, odd teeth, horn-like excrescences, rudimentary organs) as provisional mysteries to be investigated rather than evidence against teleology. Example: the spleen has prompted hypotheses until a correct function is found. Anti-pattern: concluding 'no purpose' and abandoning further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain exceptions via unity of type and homology (unité de plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rare and surprising exceptions to the rule of design (rudimentary organs, sexual differences, loss of organs in some species) are to be explained by the inner connection among phenomena through the unity of the underlying nature and by the anatomical element or fundamental type (homology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for anomalies by reference to shared plan/type rather than random failure: e.g., vestigial male breasts, eyes without openings, tadpole tails in non-swimming species. Use homology and 'unité de plan' as the structural basis upon which teleology builds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize final causes over efficient causes for understanding organic form and function
rubrics_metrics.description: In organised nature final causes (ends) give the principal clue; efficient causes assume a subordinate role as the tools of final causes. For many physiological questions, knowledge of the final cause is more instructive than the efficient cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: knowing the end (blood goes to lungs for oxidation and returns to nourish) is more illuminating than identifying the efficient mechanism of circulation. Evaluation: explanations that supply clear final-causes analyses are preferred; absence of efficient-mechanism detail is acceptable if the final cause is well established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit final causes to be treated as motives acting prior to their apprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Final causes may be conceived as motives which act upon a being before they are apprehended by intellect — 'the final cause is a motive which acts upon a being, by which it is not known.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically allow teleological causal language that attributes formative influence to ends/motives even where no prior cognition exists. Examples provided: termite nests as motive for antbear muzzle, egg-shell as motive for horny beak-point, optical laws as motive shaping the eye. Anti-pattern: requiring conscious foresight or intellect in nature to account for teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphic/intellectual explanations of natural design
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not impute the limitation of human intellect (design produced by conception of ends) to nature; nature accomplishes regularity and apparent design without the guidance of intellect or reflection—eg., a snowflake 'measured' without mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that posit an external intelligence 'like ours' engineering natural forms (Anaxagoras-style). Favor accounts that locate design in the will's manifestation rather than in intellective planning. Use analogies (snowflake, printing) to diagnose anthropomorphic error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homology and comparative anatomy as foundational material for teleological work
rubrics_metrics.description: The homology (unité de plan) revealed in comparative anatomy (e.g., same number of cervical vertebrae, analogues between human arm and whale fin) supplies the material upon which teleology operates and constrains teleological explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building teleological explanations, incorporate homological relations as the pre-given structural framework; teleology explains modifications of this plan, not arbitrary departures. Examples: Richard Owen's 'Ostéologie comparée' and Geoffroy St. Hilaire's 'anatomical element.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When analyzing an organ, enumerate its distinct final causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain specific organs by setting out their ends: e.g., the corolla's ends are (1) protection of pistil and stamina, (2) preparation and concentration of purified saps into pollen and germs, (3) production of essential oil/fragrant vapour to protect reproductive parts from damp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-point final-cause lists as the model for organ analysis. Evaluation: a good teleological account will clearly enumerate and justify the multiple purposes an organ serves rather than offer vague or single-purpose accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of efficient causes (qualitas occulta) and the sufficiency of final causes within their sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Every efficient cause ultimately rests upon something unfathomable (a force of nature, qualitas occulta) and therefore gives only relative explanation, whereas the final cause within its sphere can afford a sufficient and perfect explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat efficient-cause explanations as inherently limited and provisional; in domains of organised nature favor final-cause explanations for sufficiency. Anti-pattern: demanding an ultimate mechanical efficient-cause account where final cause already provides satisfactory understanding.
